name: Belgian French
notes: Belgian French as a thin variant of Metropolitan French (fr-FR). It inherits every table, rule and word exception of fr-FR and states only what a cited source states. LOW VOWELS: ⟨â⟩ is [aː]. The PFC survey of Tournai (PFC vowel page, d) 1)) lists Tournai under 'rat = ras' and under 'patte ≠ pâte (opposition de longueur)', introduced by 'Parfois, la distinction entre les deux voyelles est substituée par une différence de longueur'. Bardiaux et al. (2016: 40) add that the /a/ ~ /ɑ/ contrast 'semble avoir disparu chez l'immense majorité des locuteurs', and that where it is kept it goes with length (patte [pat] vs pâte [pɑːt]); the spec keeps the Tournai value. CIRCUMFLEX ⟨ê⟩: [ɛː] in a final syllable closed by a pronounced consonant (FR_BE_CIRC_E_LONG: fête [fɛːt], rêve [ʁɛːv]), short elsewhere (fêter [fɛte], forêt [fɔʁɛ]). Bardiaux et al. (2016: 40): 'fête [fɛːt] s'oppose encore à faites [fɛt]'; Avanzi (2024, Oxford Handbook ch. 14: 425-426): the faites ~ fête length contrast is phonological for everyone in the French-speaking regions of Belgium. FINAL MUTE ⟨e⟩ AFTER A VOWEL: the vowel is long (rules FR_BE_FINAL_E_LONG and FR_BE_FINAL_E_LONG_UI: aimée [ɛmeː], vie [viː], nue [nyː], bleue [bløː], joie [ʒwaː], pluie [plwiː]), after the PFC e-caduc page (section 'Français de Suisse et de Belgique') and Bardiaux et al. (2016: 39-40). GLIDE: [ɥi] is [wi] (rule FR_BE_UI_W: lui [lwi], nuit [nwi]), after Bardiaux et al. (2016: 41), with the context from Wikipedia only (see the rule note). huit reads [wi] and not [wit] because fr-FR does not yet give huit its final [t]. VINGT: [vɛ̃t] with its final [t] in isolation (word exception). The PFC consonant page (II d) 4)) records [vɛ̃t] at Gembloux and [vɛ̃] at Liège; the Français de nos régions survey (Avanzi 2016, map 'vingt') puts the share of [vɛ̃t] in the Belgian provinces at about 50 to 90 per cent, higher than anywhere in France outside the north and east, and Avanzi (2024, Sprachenräume der Schweiz: 117) says Belgium pronounces the final -t of vingt. The /ɛ̃/ ~ /œ̃/ contrast (brin ≠ brun) is kept as in fr-FR; Bardiaux et al. (2016: 40) say only half of the speakers in recent surveys still make it. NOT MODELLED: the long vowel before a plural ⟨-es⟩ (aimées), the palatal appendix after a long vowel among older speakers (épée [epeːj], Bardiaux et al. 2016: 40), diaeresis (nier [ni.je]), [w] for [ɥ] before [ɛ̃] (Wikipedia only), word-final devoicing in the Walloon area and the long, high penultimate syllable of the Liège region (Bardiaux et al. 2016: 41-42), the opening of /e ɛ o ɔ/ among older speakers at Liège and Gembloux, [h] for ⟨h⟩ among older speakers at Liège, vowel quality in general, and the numerals septante and nonante (numbers are out of scope). The sources describe several Belgian varieties; this spec states the features they give for Belgium as a whole.

sources.author: Projet PFC (Phonologie du français contemporain), FLORAL-PFC
sources.title: Le français expliqué: Prononciation, I. Le système vocalique, d) Variation
sources.notes: READ (open web page; the page metadata gives 2010 as its publication year and 2017 as its last change). The page reports, from PFC survey points: patte ≠ pâte by LENGTH at Neuchâtel (Switzerland) and Tournai (Belgium) and by timbre at Nyon; patte = pâte at Brunoy and Abidjan; brin ≠ brun kept at Tournai and Nyon (very slight timbre difference), at Toulouse and Abidjan (marked), and fading among young speakers at Neuchâtel; the length opposition faites [fɛt] ~ fête [fɛːt], belle ~ bêle, nu ~ nue, vit ~ vie at Neuchâtel. The page cites Gadet (1996) and Léon (2007).

sources.author: Bardiaux, A., Racine, I., Simon, A.C. & Hambye, P.
sources.title: Le français en Belgique
sources.publisher: In Detey, S., Racine, I., Kawaguchi, Y. & Eychenne, J. (eds.), La prononciation du français dans le monde : du natif à l'apprenant. Paris: CLE International
sources.notes: READ (open PDF in the UCLouvain DIAL repository). p. 39-40: vowel length is phonological in a final open syllable, especially in feminine forms (soutenu [sutny] vs soutenue [sutnyː], compagnie [kɔ̃paniː]); fête [fɛːt] vs faites [fɛt]; the /a/ ~ /ɑ/ contrast has gone for most speakers, and with length where kept (pâte [pɑːt]); brin ≠ brun for half of the speakers. p. 40: an appendix [j] after a long vowel among older speakers (épée [epeːj]). p. 41: diaeresis; [w] where France has [ɥ] (huit [wit]) but never *[mwɛt] for muette; word-final devoicing in the Walloon area. p. 42: the Liège penultimate syllable and the opening of vowels at Liège and Gembloux.

sources.author: Projet PFC (Phonologie du français contemporain), FLORAL-PFC
sources.title: Le français expliqué: Prononciation, II. Le système consonantique, d) Variation
sources.notes: READ (open web page, page 3 of the pronunciation pages). Section II d) 4): the numeral vingt is said [vɛ̃t] at Nyon and Genève (Switzerland) and at Gembloux (Belgium), and [vɛ̃] at Québec, Marseille, Bamako, Liège and Brunoy. Section II d) 3): diaeresis is common in Swiss and Belgian French.

sources.author: Projet PFC (Phonologie du français contemporain), FLORAL-PFC
sources.title: Le e caduc : variation géographique
sources.notes: READ (open web page; the page metadata gives 2008-12-01 as its publication date and 2017-10-26 as its last change). Section 'Français de Suisse et de Belgique': a final e after a vowel (amie, jolie, jouée) survives as a lengthening of the vowel before it: ami [ami] vs amie [amiː], joué [ʒue] vs jouée [ʒueː], bleu [blø] vs bleue [bløː]; the lengthening is often a diphthong (épée [epei], a Swiss speaker).

sources.author: Avanzi, M.
sources.title: vingT et moinS
sources.publisher: Français de nos régions (blog of the survey project)
sources.notes: READ (open web page and its map 29_vingt.png, survey Euro-2, close to 10,000 respondents). The share of respondents who say vingt with its final [t] is highest in the north and east of France, in Switzerland and in Belgium; on the map the Swiss cantons are at about 90 to 100 per cent and the Belgian provinces at about 50 to 90 per cent.

sources.author: Avanzi, M.
sources.title: Regional variation in the French of France
sources.publisher: In The Oxford Handbook of the French Language, ch. 14. Oxford University Press (uncorrected first proofs read)
sources.notes: READ (uncorrected proofs in the Neuchâtel LIBRA repository; page numbers are the proof's). p. 423: in southern mainland France the loi de position applies. p. 422: the south does not keep piqué ~ piquet apart (both [e]). p. 424: a circumflex triggers a long vowel in the north-eastern regions of France (a statement about France, not about Belgium or Switzerland). pp. 425-426: the faites ~ fête length contrast is phonological for everyone in the French-speaking regions of Belgium and most of French-speaking Switzerland (except Valais).

sources.author: Avanzi, M.
sources.title: Français
sources.publisher: In Glaser, E., Kabatek, J. & Sonnenhauser, B. (eds.), Sprachenräume der Schweiz, Band 1: Sprachen. Tübingen: Narr Francke Attempto
sources.notes: READ (open access, CC BY-SA 4.0). pp. 115-116: the quantity contrast of nu/nue, mettre/maître and bout/boue still holds fairly well in French-speaking Switzerland, whatever the canton; in Vaud (and parts of Geneva and Lower Valais) the long vowel can take a palatal off-glide (année [-eːj]), and n. 8 adds a diphthong after [i] and a schwa after [u] or [y]. p. 114: patte ~ pâte is kept by length. p. 117: vingt is said with a final -t 'dans toute la Suisse, comme en Belgique et dans le grand est de la France'.

ancestors.notes: Standard Metropolitan French, the base of every other variety here.

allophone_rules.notes: FR_BE_FINAL_E_LONG and FR_BE_UI_W together, for ⟨ui⟩ before a word-final mute ⟨e⟩ (pluie [plwiː], suie). It stands first because one slot takes only the first rule that matches.

[ɥ] is [w] in the unit ⟨ui⟩ [ɥi]: huit [wit], lui [lwi], nuit [nwi]. Bardiaux et al. (2016: 41): 'les variétés belges connaissent souvent [w] là où en FR on trouve [ɥ] (ex. huit [wit])', and [ɥ] stays an allophone of /y/ elsewhere ('muette peut être prononcé [mɥɛt] ou [my.ɛt] mais jamais *[mwɛt]'). The source gives one example and states no context. WIKIPEDIA-ONLY for the context, before [i]: English Wikipedia, Belgian French, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_French, revision 1386277100 (2026-11-17), 'Traditional French's diphthongs /ɥi, ɥɛ̃/ which are replaced by [wi, wæ̃]' (it cites Hambye & Simon 2009: 106, not opened here); French Wikipedia, Français de Belgique, https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ais_de_Belgique, revision 241690655 (2026-11-26), 'absence de la semi-voyelle /ɥ/, remplacée par /w/ devant /i/ (« huit » /wit/) et par /y/ ailleurs'. The two editions agree on [w] before [i]; they differ on [ɥɛ̃], which the English edition alone lists and this spec does not model.

A vowel before a word-final mute ⟨e⟩ is long, the vowel of a unit such as ⟨oi⟩ [wa] included (joie [ʒwaː], soie): the ⟨e⟩ survives as the length of the vowel before it (PFC, Le e caduc : variation géographique, section 'Français de Suisse et de Belgique': ami [ami] vs amie [amiː], joué [ʒue] vs jouée [ʒueː], bleu [blø] vs bleue [bløː]; Bardiaux et al. 2016: 39-40: soutenu [sutny] vs soutenue [sutnyː], compagnie [kɔ̃paniː]). The ⟨e⟩ must end the word, so a plural ⟨-es⟩ keeps the short vowel here (NOT MODELLED).

⟨ê⟩ is long [ɛː] in a final syllable closed by a pronounced consonant (Bardiaux et al. (2016: 40): 'certains mots ont conservé leur voyelle historiquement longue. Ainsi, fête [fɛːt] s'oppose encore à faites [fɛt]', in a paragraph on length in the final syllable). The sources give the length only in such a final syllable, so ⟨ê⟩ elsewhere keeps the fr-FR [ɛ]: fêter [fɛte], bêtise, forêt [fɔʁɛ].
